body: Natalia Katona is a freelance commodity analyst, based in the United Arab Emirates. Situated off California’s Santa Barbara coast, the Santa Ynez project operated by Sable Offshore has become a litmus test of President Trump’s determination to revive oil production in a state pursuing a future beyond it. After a decade of shutdowns, its return depended on the Trump administration’s intervention in a prolonged regulatory battle. Originally developed by ExxonMobil, the Santa Ynez complex comprises the Hondo, Harmony and Heritage platforms and their associated onshore infrastructure. Its troubles began in May 2015, when Plains All American’s Line 901 pipeline ruptured due to external corrosion near Refugio State Beach, spilling almost 3,000 barrels of crude . The failure cut off the project’s route to local refineries and broader market, forcing production to stop. ExxonMobil eventually sold the assets to Sable in 2024 for a total consideration of $643 million . Restarting the production proved difficult. Pipeline safety requirements, permitting disputes and court orders kept the development from returning to normal operations. Those obstacles unfolded against Democrat-led California’s broader push to reduce its dependence on fossil fuels: in 2021, Governor Gavin Newsom asked state regulators to analyze how to phase out oil extraction by 2045 . Sable announced in May 2025 that it had restarted production from Harmony, a claim California officials disputed , saying the activity was well testing. The offshore platforms sit in federal waters, beyond the state’s direct reach, but the oil initially went into storage while its onshore pipeline route, which California regulated at the time, remained blocked. The Trump administration then helped reopen that route in two steps. In December 2025, the federal Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) reclassified the onshore pipelines as interstate infrastructure at Sable’s request, asserting federal oversight, and approved their restart plan on Dec. 22 . After the conflict between the US and Iran started in late February 2026, just as the ensuing energy crisis hit the markets, Energy Secretary Chris Wright invoked the Defense Production Act to direct the restoration of operations on March 13 , citing supply risks and military dependence on foreign oil. Sable resumed pipeline shipments the following day. However, California’s Democratic administration challenged both interventions, turning the project’s revival into a continuing fight over federal and state authority. Democratic control of the House and Senate, won in the early November midterms , will not automatically reverse those decisions. The new Congress takes office in January, while Trump retains executive authority and the ability to veto legislation. But congressional committees can investigate the administration’s intervention, demand records and use spending negotiations to seek restrictions. Members of California’s congressional delegation have already started: in May they wrote to Sable’s CEO asking the company to preserve records and promising continued oversight in the next Congress. For Sable, the likely exposure is greater scrutiny and less scope for additional legislative support, rather than an immediate congressional shutdown. Courts remain the more direct threat to the legal foundations of its pipeline operations. On Tuesday, the BLS reported Core CPI at 0.3% , above the expected 0.2%, and CPI m/m at 0.4%, higher than the expected 0.3% for the month of October. This continues to be a thorn in the side of doves, and should continue to put pressure on the Fed to remain restrictive. Fridayâs labor report gave the market an additional policy input that shouldnât be ignored. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that nonfarm payroll employment increased by 165,000 jobs in October, while the unemployment rate came in at 4.1%. The labor market is still expanding, which can reduce pressure for rapid monetary easing, although payrolls alone donât determine Federal Reserve policy. Nonetheless, more employment typically means that more consumers are out there, with inflation having that input. For gold, the overall relevant information runs through expected policy rates, nominal Treasury yields, inflation compensation, and the dollar, rather than just through employment itself. A higher inflation reading supports goldâs store-of-wealth narrative, but it could also lift yields if investors expect a firmer policy path. A softer reading could reduce nominal and real yields while also weakening demand for inflation protection. The shape of the real yield curve also deserves attention. On November 6, the 30-year real yield was 3.07%, above the 20-year rate of 2.91% and the 10-year rate of 2.63%. This upward slope implies investors demand progressively more inflation-adjusted return at longer maturities. For the gold market, the long end can matter through portfolio allocation and the cost of carrying defensive positions. A fall confined to short maturities would be less supportive than a broad decline across the entire curve. Strong productivity can allow output and wages to grow with less inflationary pressure, potentially modifying and moderating the monetary premium embedded in gold. title: Gold Price Recovers Above US$4,000 As Analysts Forecast Further Gains - DirectorsTalk Interviews
body: Gold prices recovered on 11 November after falling sharply in the previous session, with the precious metal holding above the US$4,000 per ounce level despite renewed concerns over inflation and the prospect of higher US interest rates. Spot gold traded around US$4,040 per ounce, following a decline of approximately 3% on Tuesday. Stronger-than-expected US inflation data and expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening had contributed to the earlier selling pressure. The latest recovery comes as analysts assess whether the recent correction represents a temporary setback or a change in the broader direction of the gold market. The US$4,000 level has emerged as an important support area, with prices managing to remain above it despite pressure from higher bond yields and a stronger US dollar. Standard Chartered maintains a positive outlook, forecasting an average gold price of US$4,650 per ounce during the fourth quarter of 2026, followed by a further increase to US$4,850 in the first quarter of 2027. The bank points to continued investment demand and central bank purchases as important sources of support. Gold-backed exchange-traded products attracted 211 tonnes of investment demand during the third quarter, their strongest quarterly inflows since 2024. A further 19 tonnes entered these products during October. Central bank purchases also remained significant, reaching 321 tonnes in the third quarter, above Standard Chartered’s estimate of 200 tonnes. Continued official-sector buying has provided an additional source of demand as central banks diversify their reserves. The bank also considers gold’s ability to maintain support above US$4,000 despite stronger economic data an indication of underlying market resilience. However, a move above US$4,200 would represent the next significant technical level to watch. CPM Group has also maintained a constructive view of the precious metals market following the recent correction. The research group considers the latest decline a period of consolidation following several days of gains, rather than evidence that the broader upward trend has ended. Its assessment points to continued demand for precious metals amid concerns surrounding economic uncertainty, government debt, inflation and geopolitical developments. Uncertainty over technology company valuations and wider financial market conditions has also contributed to interest in alternative stores of value. body: Advanced Micro Devices Inc. shares jumped 9.5% on Wednesday. Strong results from AI cloud provider CoreWeave and an upbeat analyst report on server processors drove a broad rally in semiconductor stocks. AMD stock traded at $564.17 in afternoon trading, up 9.50%. It outpaced Nvidia, which gained about 5%. The move added to a sharp rebound from last week's AI selloff. The rally began after CoreWeave reported third-quarter results late Tuesday that beat analyst forecasts. The company reported revenue of $3.66 billion and raised its full-year 2026 revenue forecast to between $13.0 billion and $13.3 billion, according to The Motley Fool. CoreWeave also said it plans capital investment of $37 billion to $39 billion. Analysts said that points to continued heavy spending on data center chips, including AMD's processors. CoreWeave shares surged more than 25%. AMD also got a boost from a UBS report on server processor sales. UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri said server CPU shipments rose 31% from a year earlier in the third quarter. He said AMD's server CPU market share held steady at about 28.4%, while Intel's share fell 2.4 percentage points. Arcuri also believes CPU prices are rising, which could boost AMD's profit margins. He projected that CPU sales could reach $210 billion by 2030. At AMD's current market share, that would mean nearly $60 billion in CPU sales for the company. AI systems increasingly need powerful central processors alongside graphics chips, which has fueled demand for AMD's EPYC server processors. Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said AI stocks were "clearly in oversold territory" and named AMD, Nvidia and Broadcom as top picks. He described AMD as "very attractive" for growth, though less compelling on valuation. AMD has a 12-month median price target of $650, based on 56 analysts, according to The Motley Fool. AMD reported record third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion earlier this month, up 45% from a year earlier and above analyst expectations. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.09, up 74% and ahead of forecasts. Management said demand exceeds supply. The company increased inventory by about $3 billion in the quarter to $11.5 billion to meet strong data center demand. Free cash flow fell to $554 million in the quarter from $1.9 billion a year earlier, which management attributed to working capital and spending on capacity. AMD pairs its Instinct AI graphics chips with EPYC server processors in its Helios rack-scale systems. Riot Platforms is one of the purest crypto infrastructure plays in this shortlist, since its large scale Bitcoin Mining segment directly secures the Bitcoin network while its engineering arm supplies power equipment into data centers and industrial projects. Riot Platforms runs U.S. Bitcoin mining facilities that support the Bitcoin network and offers data center hosting, while its engineering segment designs and manufactures electrical and power distribution gear. Bitcoin Mining produced about US$473 million in revenue versus roughly US$176 million from Engineering, and the group carries a market cap of about US$6.8b. "Riot Platforms is building on its earlier plan to grow a scalable data center business by locking in a 20-year, 191 MW lease with a frontier AI lab and expanding AMD's lease to 50 MW. This supports expectations for higher recurring revenue and operating lease margins as contracted data center revenue of about US$9.8b flows into earnings over time." The real swing factor is how a single financing and execution choice shapes the gap between those projected lease flows and actual long term margins. body: This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) trades at $177.22, and Wall Street’s average price target is $325.78. At that price, the target means 83.83% upside. Most of that gap opened over five sessions. By our calculation, the stock fell 18.29% from a $206.69 close. Based on Tuesday’s $4.08 trillion market value and 24.15 billion shares, we estimate about $913 billion of value was erased. Tuesday’s $168.89 close was the stock’s lowest since a $165.17 finish in late March. A gap this wide usually signals that analysts and the market disagree about something basic. Here, the disagreement is over governance and China exposure, even as NVIDIA says demand for its chips still outpaces supply. Earnings come out November 17 after the close. That report will be the first hard test of whether the targets or the stock price is closer to right. This was NVIDIA’s worst five-session stretch since the one that ended September 1, 2022. In that stretch, the split-adjusted stock fell 22.2%, from $17.91 to $13.94. A window that ended in April 2022 was also worse, with a 19.89% drop, so “since 2022” means since that September. The DeepSeek comparison sets five days against five days. NVIDIA lost 16.97% in a single January 2025 session, falling from $142.62 to $118.42. Its worst five sessions around that shock cost 15.89%. This week’s slide was also bigger than the 17.22% drop over the five sessions that ended in September 2024. No single day came close to the DeepSeek session. The worst was a 9.26% fall to $181.60. The lone up day, a 2.78% bounce to $186.64, did not hold; other sessions fell 3.17% to $200.13 and 4.27% to $178.67. On Tuesday, it lost $9.78, or 5.47%, on 429.2 million shares, trading as low as $165.89. NVIDIA’s independent directors hired Joon H. Kim, a former acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, along with Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. They will investigate reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort . The board says it has no reason to believe national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised. A separate report detailed the hardware transfers. At least $7.5 billion of NVIDIA hardware has reached Chinese companies since 2023 through a network linked to businesswoman Alice Huang, who is not related to the CEO. The stock also faced a broader tech sell-off and an inflation report that came in above forecasts. October consumer prices rose 0.4%, and core prices rose 0.3%, which hurts high-multiple stocks most. The 2022 slide also had a China trigger. NVIDIA announced new export license rules. The rules for its A100 and H100 chips, it said, could cost about $400 million in China sales that quarter. That recovery had to wait for the chip cycle to turn, and the DeepSeek drop reversed once buyers decided cheaper, more efficient AI would increase demand for chips. Of 62 analysts, 10 rate NVIDIA Strong Buy, 49 Buy, two Hold, and one Sell. Measured from Tuesday’s close, the consensus target means 92.89% upside. Price targets are estimates, though, and they often lag fast-moving news. Baird downgraded the stock to Neutral from Outperform and cut its target to $200 from $500. It cited uncertainty over Huang’s tenure and the chance that large cloud companies spend less on AI in 2027. Analyst Tristan Gerra estimated that a possible new H200 export ban to China could mean a $5 billion write-down. Morgan Stanley removed NVIDIA as a Top Pick. It kept its Overweight rating and $300 target, and Bank of America dropped it from its top-ideas list. Business results remain strong: revenue rose 105.8% last quarter to $96.22 billion, and the stock trades at about 11 times forward earnings. NVIDIA’s decline was specific to the company. Over the same five sessions, Advanced Micro Devices ( NASDAQ:AMD ) gained 6.47%, and Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ) slipped 0.
